Overview

It's important to break down Baku's plan and understand his perspective before diving into the details. Baku's main goal was to defeat Hal using a "leap second" that was going to happen on January 1st at exactly 9:00 a.m. Baku wanted to use that leap second to his advantage. At the start of the game, his first step was to figure out the pace of the game—this is important because he needed to know how fast or slow things were happening. Once he had a good grasp of the pace, his next move was to get into the leap second route.

Now, after entering the leap second route, Baku had to make sure that Hal stayed in a near-death state for at least five minutes. The reason for this is that, in the game, the container or limit for being near death is five minutes. Once someone has been in that state for five minutes, it’s almost guaranteed they will die because surviving after that point is nearly impossible. So, to make sure his plan worked, Baku’s goal was for Hal to reach that five-minute mark during the leap second. If Hal didn’t reach or exceed that limit, the whole strategy would fail, and there’d be no point in using the leap second at all. This is why Baku was so focused on ensuring that Hal would be near death for at least five minutes.
What is Leap Second?

Now, let’s talk about the leap second route. If you’re not familiar with what that means, it’s pretty simple. The leap second route is the specific time Baku could take his turn as the dropper, which was at 8:59 a.m. If he could play at exactly that time, he was in the leap second route. But if he missed it, he wasn’t in the route anymore.

To figure out if he was in the leap second route, Baku had to calculate whether his turns would land him there. Each half of a round in the game takes two minutes. If we assume Baku played a turn at 8:17 a.m., he would have to check if 8:59 a.m. was part of his turns. Baku’s turns happen every four minutes, so if you calculate forward from 8:17 a.m., you see he wouldn’t make it to 8:59 a.m. However, if you start calculating from 8:35 a.m., he would be able to take his turn right at 8:59 a.m., meaning he was in the leap second route. This timing is critical to Baku’s strategy because everything depended on him making his move in that exact second.
Hals PoV of Leap Second:

Now let’s look at Hal’s perspective. Right from the start, Hal knew about the leap second. In chapter 473, Baku gives Hal a stopwatch, and when Hal starts it, he sees it ticking from 59 milliseconds to 60 milliseconds. This tiny detail was a clue to Hal about the leap second, and during this time, he noticed Baku’s hand trembling slightly. That tremor was unusual, and Hal became suspicious. From this, Hal started to figure out that the leap second was central to Baku’s plan.

To test his theory, Hal gave the stopwatch back to Baku, and if you look closely at the top corner of the panel, Hal stopped the watch at exactly 9 seconds, another hint about the leap second at 9:00 a.m. Hal used this as a trap to see how Baku would react, and when Baku broke the stopwatch, it confirmed Hal’s suspicions. From this, Hal figured out Baku’s whole scheme.

However, Hal did something interesting after figuring out the leap second. He erased the memory of it from his mind, using what’s called his "perfect mode." Even though Hal consciously erased the memory, his subconscious still remembered it. This was a risky move, but it was part of Hal’s plan to try and deal with the leap second without relying on his conscious memory of it. Even though Hal forgot about the leap second, his instincts and subconscious were still working, so he could react even without directly remembering the details.

Hal’s plan from here was to avoid the leap second, but he knew there was a chance he could forget about it entirely because he erased his memory. That was the main risk he took in his strategy, but he still believed he could rely on his subconscious to remember and react in time.
Rules:
The two people alternate between being the Dropper ("D") and the Checker ("C").
"D" must drop the handkerchief within 1 minute, but it's fine to drop it instantly.
"C" must check if the handkerchief has been dropped within 1 minute, with the last second possible being right as it hits 1 minute.
If "D" has not dropped the handkerchief within 1 minute, "D" loses.
The least possible allotted time of Near Death Drug is 1 second.
A failed check (meaning the handkerchief was not yet dropped) instantly adds 1 minute of Near Death Drug, which is then injected together with the other allotted time.
For example, if you have 11 seconds of Near Death Drug allotted already and fail the check, you'll then be injected with 71 seconds (1 minute 11 seconds) of Near Death Drug.
If 5 minutes of Near Death Drug is allotted, it's instantly injected.

Once the allotted time of the Near Death Drug is complete, CPR is applied for 10 seconds along with a shot of adrenaline by the referee. These are the only methods that will be allowed to attempt to revive a person.
After being revived, a short rest of about 2 minutes is applied before the next round of the game.
The Analysis:

In order to avoid Baku’s trap and still have a chance to win, Hal’s only possible strategy is, ironically, to fall into Baku’s trap but still manage to survive after the leap second has passed. At first glance, this might seem counterintuitive or illogical, but if we examine it closely, it makes perfect sense. The core of Hal’s strategy lies in his understanding that Baku’s plan doesn’t extend beyond the leap second. Once that moment has passed, Baku will be vulnerable, as he hasn’t accounted for what happens next. Hal can exploit this gap, but first, he must survive the trap that Baku has laid.

However, to do this, Hal needs to keep his total time of death (TTD) under five minutes. As we discussed earlier, if anyone in the game reaches or exceeds five minutes of TTD, survival is nearly impossible. Additionally, Hal is aware of the irregular memory loss he’s suffering from, which could strike at any time and leave him exposed. This factor makes it even harder for him to outmaneuver Baku, as forgetting key details at the wrong time could seal his fate.

The only way for Hal to counter Baku’s leap second trap is to, in fact, walk into it knowingly. This is where Hal’s foresight comes into play: he understands that, due to his memory loss, he is likely to forget about the leap second and fall into the trap automatically. But what makes Hal’s strategy brilliant is his decision to prepare for this in advance. Instead of trying to avoid the trap, he embraces the inevitability of falling into it. He decides that his best course of action is to survive, even after dying during the leap second. To do this, he must keep his TTD below the critical five-minute mark. As long as Hal doesn't exceed or even reach five minutes of near-death time, there’s a chance he can recover and win the game, even after falling for Baku’s ploy.

Hal is smart enough to know that this is only a possible scenario, not a guaranteed outcome. There’s a chance that he might not lose his memory during the leap second at all, but he prepares for the worst-case scenario just in case. His ability to think ahead and prepare for every eventuality, even the most unlikely ones, is a testament to his cunning. This approach ensures that, whether he loses his memory or not, his preparations won’t be wasted. Hal is always thinking a few steps ahead, anticipating different outcomes and adjusting his strategy accordingly.

Now, Baku could theoretically counter this if he notices Hal’s TTD. If Baku realizes that Hal’s TTD isn’t long enough for the leap second to be lethal, he might abandon the leap second plan entirely. In fact, Baku is pragmatic enough that he wouldn’t hesitate to switch tactics if he sees that the leap second is no longer a viable way to defeat Hal. This introduces a new layer of risk to Hal’s plan. Not only does he have to survive the leap second, but he also has to prevent Baku from realizing that the leap second won’t work. If Baku figures it out, he’ll abandon the plan, and Hal will lose his advantage.

To avoid this, Hal’s plan becomes even riskier. He has to create a brief yet subtle deviation in his actions that Baku won’t notice. Hal must appear as though he’s completely unaware of the leap second, making Baku believe that the leap second is still a crucial part of the game. By doing this, Hal can ensure that Baku continues relying on the leap second, giving Hal the opportunity to create that short deviation and survive. This delicate balance—acting unaware while subtly manipulating the situation—is what makes Hal’s strategy so risky yet so ingenious.

With both players’ motives now clear, we can examine the actual gameplay without any further delay. As Baku, Hal, and the referee, Yakou, enter the Obelisk, yakou notices Kaji and Marco nearby and asks them to leave. This is all part of Baku’s plan. Baku manipulates Yakou into believing that Kaji might have tampered with the clock, which leads yakou to choose the speaking clock. Baku has orchestrated this perfectly, knowing that the speaking clock is superior to anything else and will ultimately decide the outcome of the game. Baku’s manipulation of the clock is critical to his leap second strategy, as the phone line connected to the clock uses the leap second version of time. This means that, when the leap second occurs, the clock will chime twice, signaling the leap second’s passage. This sound will trigger Hal to turn around just one second before Baku drops the handkerchief.
The Real Game:

Now, let’s delve into the actual game itself. Baku and Hal decide to play a game of rock-paper-scissors to determine who will take the Dropper role, also known as the “D” role. The Dropper role has a significant advantage, so both players are keen to win. In the first round, Hal wins the rock-paper-scissors game and gets to play as the Dropper, while Baku takes the Checker role, also known as “C.” The game officially starts at 8:12 a.m., and both players immediately begin trying to read each other’s thoughts and intentions.

At this point, Hal is focused on understanding Baku’s psychology. He believes that Baku, being a gambler by nature, will take risks, including risking his own life. Hal thinks that Baku is the type of person who would turn around in the middle of the game just to experience the thrill of near-death. Based on this assumption, Hal decides not to drop the handkerchief during this phase of the game. Meanwhile, Baku is trying to read Hal’s intentions as well. He knows that Hal is incredibly sharp and would anticipate a bold move from him, but Baku also sees through Hal’s assumption.

This intricate mind game is where the real battle takes place. Both players are trying to outthink each other, anticipating their opponent’s next move while simultaneously hiding their true intentions. It’s a high-stakes psychological duel, where one misstep could lead to disaster.

Baku’s decision to intentionally die during this round is a calculated risk, designed to help him fully grasp the pace and rhythm of the game. He realizes that by experiencing a failed check, he can gather crucial information about how much time passes between different game intervals. A failed check has different timing than a successful one, and Baku understands that if he is going to fully map out the leap second route and predict Hal’s moves, he needs to know these intervals precisely. Baku opts to die here because it’s the safest form of near-death, a choice that makes sense in the context of the game since it doesn’t risk his long-term survival, while still giving him the information he needs. This also positions him advantageously, setting the game’s timeline forward by five minutes, which is important as 8:59 a.m. is still far off from the current round.

Baku’s next move is brilliant in its precision: he checks right before Hal is even able to drop the handkerchief. This means that Baku didn’t just react quickly, he actually predicted when Hal would make his move and timed his check to counter it, making sure that he would fail the check at the perfect moment. However, Hal also plays incredibly smart here. Instead of immediately dropping the handkerchief, Hal slowly places it down as a way to throw off Baku’s heightened senses. Hal knows that Baku’s god-like intuition and sensory perception could detect the exact moment he drops the handkerchief. By placing it down slowly, Hal creates a deceptive tactic designed to counter Baku’s instincts. Hal waits for Baku to check before fully committing to dropping the handkerchief, showing that he’s not just reacting but strategically anticipating Baku’s incredible abilities.

When Baku fails his check, he’s injected with the penalty drug, which will keep him in a near-death state for one minute. Meanwhile, Hal takes advantage of Baku’s vulnerability by trying to break Baku’s willpower through mental warfare. Hal makes a brilliant move by threatening Baku with tough words, trying to plant the idea in Baku’s mind that he’s already preparing to use the near-death drug again. This psychological pressure is Hal’s way of making Baku afraid of what’s coming, potentially destabilizing his mental state. However, Baku recovers from near-death at exactly 8:14 a.m., 40 seconds into the minute. The next round will begin at 8:17 a.m., and Baku quickly calculates that the interval between a failed check and the next round is about five minutes—three minutes for the injection and revival process, and two minutes for the interval before the next round starts.

Before Baku took the death drug, he removed his coat, setting up his next strategy for the following round. Now it’s 8:17 a.m., and Baku’s turn to play as the Dropper begins. As the Dropper, Baku immediately begins setting up a mind game designed to confuse Hal. He steps in front of Hal, revealing only part of his necktie and his left hand, which is carefully angled to make it appear as though he might be holding the handkerchief. By removing his coat earlier, Baku creates ambiguity, leaving Hal to question whether Baku is holding the handkerchief or the necktie. This subtle trick is designed to mess with Hal’s perception and force him to waste time trying to figure out what’s happening. In the meantime, Baku has already started accumulating Hal’s near-death drug, positioning himself to make the leap second more lethal when the time comes.

Hal, meanwhile, starts piecing together the clues that Baku has given him, slowly realizing that Baku hasn’t shown his front because he’s trying to create a mental trap. Hal begins to suspect that Baku isn’t holding the handkerchief at all but is instead using the necktie as a decoy. However, just as Hal figures this out, Baku reveals a new piece of information: he is, in fact, holding the necktie, forcing Hal to reconsider his next move. Hal holds back, waiting for one more crucial piece of information before making his final decision. He knows that Baku is playing a high-level mind game, and any rash move could cost him the game.

Then, at the exact 26th second, Hal turns around. Up until this point, Hal had been preparing to check at precisely two seconds, but Baku’s timing was impeccable. Baku had dropped the handkerchief and stepped in front of Hal at the perfect moment, preventing Hal from achieving an immediate check. The brilliance of this maneuver cannot be understated—Baku’s ability to step in front of Hal just as he was about to turn shows a level of prediction and anticipation that borders on supernatural.

But Hal isn’t far behind in this mind game. He uses abductive reasoning to create a theory based on Baku’s previous actions. Hal recalls that in the first round, Baku turned around at the exact moment he was about to drop the handkerchief. If Baku’s senses are truly as heightened as they seem, then Baku would only step in front of Hal if he had already dropped the handkerchief. Using this deductive logic, Hal concludes that Baku must have dropped the handkerchief during this round as well. This level of reasoning is a testament to Hal’s intelligence—he’s able to figure out Baku’s strategy in real-time, building a theory that not only explains Baku’s actions but also gives Hal the advantage moving forward.

Hal’s theory is confirmed when he realizes that Baku stepped in front of him to prevent a perfect check. This revelation allows Hal to see through Baku’s motives and understand that Baku had dropped the handkerchief while simultaneously trying to confuse him. Through this process of reasoning, Hal accumulates 24 seconds of near-death drug, which, while not yet enough to trigger the leap second’s lethal effects, puts him one step closer to the endgame.

Meanwhile, Baku’s situation grows more intense as the stakes rise in the second half of this complex game. With 60 seconds of total time of death (TTD) accumulated, Baku has already survived close calls, but the battle of wits between him and Hal is far from over. To fully understand Baku’s predicament, we must first analyze Hal’s earlier decision to check at the 2-second mark, a move that seems peculiar given his otherwise cautious and strategic nature. Why would Hal make such an uncharacteristically risky bet? The answer lies in his deep understanding of the situation and his opponent.

Hal made the bold decision to check early because he knows something crucial: Baku cannot afford to let him die at this stage of the game. If Hal dies now, it could collapse the potential leap second route, a situation that Baku is keen to avoid. Baku’s entire strategy revolves around managing Hal’s near-death accumulation while keeping himself alive long enough to manipulate the leap second to his advantage. Hal, being aware of this, consciously decides to check at a point where he knows Baku will hesitate to drop the handkerchief too early. Baku, for his part, understands that any irregularity at this point could disrupt the game’s timing, so he holds back. But even with these insights, Baku’s near-supernatural perception allows him to avoid Hal’s perfect check. As a result, Hal ends up accumulating 24 seconds of near-death drug, an effective but still incomplete accumulation.

Now, with the second half of the second round about to begin at 8:19 a.m., the game’s dynamics shift again. Baku plays as C, while Hal takes on the role of D. At this moment, both players understand the critical importance of the leap second route. If Baku intends to enter this route, he must intentionally fail his check in this round. A failed check would advance the game by five minutes, positioning Baku’s next turn as the Dropper at 8:24 a.m., placing him in a prime position to manipulate the leap second. However, if Baku fails here, it could also ruin the possibility of using the leap second effectively in later rounds. Therefore, Baku faces a difficult choice: succeed in this check and maintain control over the game’s pace, or fail the check and risk jeopardizing his strategic path.

Hal, knowing the significance of the leap second, tries once again to rattle Baku’s mental state. Hal is fully aware that his own worst-case scenario is his impending memory loss, which will make it increasingly difficult for him to keep track of his moves and the game’s intricacies. But even in this vulnerable state, Hal has another way to win: break Baku’s concentration and force him into making a fatal mistake. To this end, Hal begins subtly testing his echolocation abilities, producing high-frequency sounds near the dropped handkerchief in an attempt to detect it without using sight. However, the sound of the speaking clock proves too loud, interfering with Hal’s echolocation.

Recognizing the need for a quieter environment, Hal uses a clever manipulation tactic to alter the game conditions. Whispering something to Baku, Hal draws the referees’ attention, causing them to lower the volume of the speaking clock in an effort to catch what Hal and Baku are saying. This gives Hal the quieter atmosphere he needs to employ echolocation more effectively. In this way, Hal demonstrates his ability to manipulate not just his opponent, but also the very environment of the game, using people who aren’t even directly involved in the match as tools in his strategy.

Now, back to Baku. Knowing that he cannot afford to die in this round, Baku opts for a safer strategy. His near-death container is emptied, meaning that he is not currently in a position to risk further accumulation. Baku believes that Hal won’t drop the handkerchief for a while, making it safe for him to adopt a more cautious approach. But this is precisely what Hal has anticipated. Hal’s original plan was to eliminate Baku before the leap second ever becomes relevant. However, Baku, recognizing Hal’s intent, counters by checking at the 60th second of the round. Hal, realizing that Baku is unlikely to turn around in the early part of the round, drops the handkerchief at the 35th second, a strategic choice based on the idea that the longer the round progresses, the less likely Baku is to check. By waiting until after 30 seconds, Hal tests whether Baku will take the bait and turn around to check. But Baku, staying true to his cautious strategy, does not check, forcing Hal to reconsider his plan of attack.

At this point, Hal begins to suspect that it may not be possible to defeat Baku simply by waiting for him to make a mistake. Baku’s consistent ability to avoid Hal’s traps and survive near-death scenarios means that Hal will need to adjust his tactics moving forward. The round concludes with Baku remaining seated, as he attempts to test whether the timing of successful checks can be altered. However, he quickly realizes that the interval between rounds is fixed at two minutes for safe checks, meaning that any attempt to change the pace of the game by remaining seated will not work.

The second half of the second round begins at 8:21 a.m., and Hal has now failed his check, leading to his first near-death revival. This marks a turning point, as Hal begins to experience the first signs of memory loss, a condition that has been looming over him since the start of the game and childhood. When Hal regains consciousness, he is confused about how he lost to Baku, and Yaku, the referee, explains that Hal failed his check at the fifth second. This detail catches Hal off guard, as he doesn’t remember why he chose to check at such an early point in the round. However, as his memory slowly returns, Hal recalls that he had challenged Baku directly but ultimately lost.

Yet, this sequence of events raises a critical question: why would Hal check at exactly 5 seconds? Challenging Baku head-on is not consistent with Hal’s usual careful approach. If Hal had intended to challenge Baku, he could have done so at any point before the 5-second mark, so why choose such a specific moment? The answer lies in a hidden strategy. It seems that Hal’s decision to check at 5 seconds was not a reckless gamble, but rather a deliberate move to fail his check intentionally.

Hal’s primary goal in failing this check was to open the leap second route for Baku. As the game progresses, it becomes clear that it is nearly impossible for Baku to make Hal die and trigger the leap second. For Baku to enter the leap second route, he must die himself, and that’s exactly what Hal sets up by failing his check in the second round. By dying, Hal advances the game by five minutes, pushing the next round to start at 8:26 a.m. At this point, it will be Baku’s turn to play as C. If Baku dies at 8:26 a.m., he will have a clear path to enter the leap second route.
